newsitem.title: JAPAN: Key facts about North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about North Korea.

text.p: Here are the main facts about North Korea.
(Note - given difficulty in obtaining official North Korean data, figures in some sections are based wholly or partly on outside sources)
AREA: 120,538 sq km (47,085 sq miles) bounded by China and the Soviet Union to the north and South Korea to the south.
CAPITAL: Pyongyang
ARMED FORCES: Active forces 1,054,000; Reserves 4,700,000.
Army - 923,000, with some 3,700 main battle tanks; 2,500 armoured personnel carriers, 10,300 artillery pieces.
Navy - 46,000, with 445 ships including 25 submarines, three frigates, and 45 missile craft.
Air Force - 85,000, including 730 combat aircraft, including 36 Su-25s and 14 MiG-29s.
Forces abroad - Advisers in some 12 African countries.
ECONOMY: Annual per capita income - $923 in 1994, down from $1,064 in 1990 (calculated at official rate of $1=2.15 North Korean won).
GNP - $21.2 billion in 1994.
Growth - Minus 1.7 percent in 1994.
Defence spending - $1.31 billion, or 2.82 billion won in 1994.

MODERN HISTORY: Soviet troops entered the northern half of Korea and U.S. troops the southern half in 1945 to disarm the Japanese, who had ruled the peninsula as a colony for 35 years until their World War Two surrender.

In 1948, following formation of the U.S.-backed Republic of Korea (ROK) in Seoul, the rival Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) was established in Pyongyang with Kim Il-sung, a Soviet-backed, anti-Japanese resistance leader, as its first prime minister. He became president in 1972.

In June 1950, North Korean armed forces entered the South in an attempt to reunite the country by force. Chinese troops later joined them to oppose U.S.-led United Nations forces. The Korean War ended with a truce signed in July 1953, but the two Koreas still remain technically at war.
During the Sino-Soviet dispute of the 1960s and 1970s, North Korea kept an equal distance between Moscow and Beijing, but later moved closer to Moscow.

At the end of the 1980s, Kim Il-sung -- alarmed as Mikhail Gorbachev's "perestroika" reforms hastened the break-up of communist East Europe and then the Soviet Union itself -- tilted back decisively towards Beijing, which was returning to hardline policies after its 1989 crackdown on dissent.

The collapse of the Soviet empire, and China's own growing need for foreign exchange, meant that Pyongyang could no longer rely on barter trade for much needed imports and its economy started on a downward spiral that has continued ever since.
While the Cold War may have ended elsewhere, it remains intractably in place on the Korean Peninsula.

In 1983, a bomb exploded in Rangoon during a visit by South Korean President Chun Doo Hwan, killing 17 Seoul officials including four cabinet ministers. Burma blamed the incident on North Korea, which vigorously denied the allegation.
Pyongyang was again consigned to international isolation four years later after the destruction of a South Korean airliner with 115 people on board near Burma in November 1987.

A captured woman who said she placed a bomb on board the ill-fated flight said she was ordered to do so by North Koreans who wanted to scare athletes and visitors away from the 1988 Olympic Games in Seoul.

In March 1994, international suspicion that North Korea might have nuclear weapons rose sharply when U.N. nuclear experts reported they had been hampered from carrying out inspection of two key nuclear sites.
By June, the United States and Seoul were leading a drive to slap North Korea with economic sanctions in an effort to force inspection of the sites.
After months of bluster, Kim defused the crisis by telling visiting former U.S. president Jimmy Carter he was ready to compromise.

He won agreement for high-level diplomatic talks with the United States, and offered an unprecedented summit meeting with the leader of the hated anti-communist South Korean state, President Kim Young-sam. They were to have met on July 25.
But Kim Il-sung's health deteriorated before the meeting took place and he died on July 8.
The death of the so-called "Great Leader" brought to de-facto power his son, the so-called "Dear Leader" Kim Jong-il, in the first communist dynastic succession.

However, North Korea's power brokers, mainly ageing military leaders from elder Kim's time, have withheld from the younger Kim the symbolic titles of head of the ruling Korean Workers Party and state president.
Kim Jong-il, faced with a collapsing economy, agreed to a deal which allowed international inspection of the North's nuclear sites in exchange for oil and building of safer nuclear power plants.
But there was no relief for Kim Jong-il when two consecutive years of record floods set off a near-famine which forced North Korea to make unprecedented appeals for international food aid.
North Korea admitted it only had half of the food needed to feed its people and relief agencies reported some peasants were eating grass to survive.
Relations with Seoul plunged to a dangerous level when a North Korean submarine ran aground during an incursion into South Korean waters last September.
Months later North Korea was forced to apologise for the incident.

Relations appeared to be just getting back on course when this month Hwang Jang-yop, the 24th-ranked official in North Korea's power structure, defected and sought asylum at the South Korean embassy in Beijing.
